dataset.name: Comparing the Recovery of Arbuscular and Ectomycorrhizal Stands from Long-Term Nitrogen Fertilization at the Fernow Experimental Forest, WV (2021 and 2022)
description: This data was generated to answer the research question: After the end of a 30-year nitrogen (N) fertilization experiment in an Eastern temperate forest, to what extent do plant microbial interactions and carbon cycling in arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) and ectomycorrhizal (ECM) dominated stands follow different recovery trajectories?

The soil and the roots used in this dataset were sampled from two watersheds (N-fertilized watershed 3 and Reference watershed 7) with 6 AM and 6 ECM dominated stands each, over the course of three months (June, July, August) in 2021 and 2022.

The "All_Roots.csv" data includes fine root biomass (in g) scaled to sampled soil (m2) (Scaled_Rt_Bm_gm2), and AM and ECM root colonization (%) in two soil fractions: the organic horizon (O) and the mineral horizon (B).

The "All_Enzymes.csv" data includes extracellular soil enzyme activity (N-acetyl-glucosaminidase (NAG), acid phosphatase (AP), β-glucosidase (BG), phenol oxidase and peroxidase), and the ratios of BG to AP (BG:AP) and BG to NAG (BG:NAG) in three soil fractions: the organic horizon (O), the bulk soil (B), and the rhizosphere (R).

The "All_Nmin" data includes inorganic N (NO3- and NH4+) pools (unit: μg of N per g of dry soil) measured pre- (I_Nitrate_ugNgsoil and I_Ammonia_ugNgsoil) and post-incubation (F_Nitrate_ugNgsoil and F_Ammonia_ugNgsoil), as well as calculated nitrification (Nitrification_day) and nitrogen mineralization (Mineralization_day) rates per day, in three soil fractions: the organic horizon (O), the bulk soil (B), and the rhizosphere (R).

measurementTechnique:
Soil Sampling and Processing
The study site is part of the Fernow Experimental Forest (herein Fernow) located in the Allegheny section of the Appalachian Mountain Range in Tucker County, West Virginia (39.03°N, 79.67°W). For our recovery study, we sampled soils from two adjacent watersheds at the Fernow: Watershed 3 which received elevated N annually at a rate of 35 kg N ha-1 in the form of ammonium sulfate ((NH₄)₂SO₄) from 1989 to 2019 (herein previously N-fertilized), and a reference watershed, Watershed 7, that received only ambient N deposition (herein reference). The watersheds used in this study had a mean annual precipitation of 1484 mm (previously N-fertilized) and 1425 mm (reference), with elevations in these watersheds ranging from 731 to 860 m (Adams et al., 2006; Edwards et al., 2011). Soils in these watersheds are well-drained coarse-textured inceptisols (loamy-skeletal, mixed mesic Typic Dystrochrept) of the Berks and Calvin Series formed from sandstone and shale (Adams et al., 2006; Gilliam et al., 1994). The tree species found in these watershed predominantly associate with AM fungi (e.g. Acer sp. and Prunus serotina), but ECM associated trees, such as sweet birch (Betula lenta), red oak (Quercus rubra), and American beech (Fagus grandifolia) are also found throughout the watersheds (Carrara et al., 2023).
We sampled soils from both watersheds for root and enzyme analysis in June, July, and August of 2021 and 2022 to capture variability across the peak of the growing season. In each watershed, we sampled a previously established network of 10 × 10 m AM– and ECM–dominated plots (Carrara et al., 2023) with six AM and six ECM dominated plots located in each watershed (N = 24 plots total). Trees of the dominant mycorrhizal type constituted more than 60% of the basal area in their respective plot. At each sampling date, we collected the organic horizon from three random 10 × 10 cm areas in each plot. Directly below these samples, we collected the top 20 cm of mineral soil using a 5 cm diameter core. The organic horizon and mineral soil samples were homogenized by plot to provide one composite organic horizon and one composite mineral soil sample for each plot.
For the organic horizon, we homogenized the samples by sieving them through an 8 mm mesh and removing the roots for biomass measurements and assessment of mycorrhizal colonization. For the mineral soil, we sieved the samples through a 2 mm mesh and separated the bulk soil from the soil aggregates adhering to the roots, which we operationally defined as the "rhizosphere" following Phillips et al. (2005). A subsample of the fresh fine roots (<2mm) was used to quantify mycorrhizal colonization (Böhm, 1979; Sutton et al., 1983). The remaining fine roots were thoroughly rinsed and dried at 65 ˚C for 72 hours to determine fine root biomass per unit area (m2). Soil gravimetric water content was determined by drying a subsample of each soil at 65 ˚C for 72 hours. The remaining soil was frozen and stored at –80 ˚C prior to enzyme analysis.

Mycorrhizal Colonization
Fine roots from AM-dominant plots were stained using trypan blue to improve the visibility of the AM structures within the roots. Prior to staining, we incubated the roots in 10% potassium hydroxide at room temperature for 48–96 hours. Next, we incubated the roots in 85% ethanol to leach any excess pigment and bleached the roots in a solution of 1-part ammonium hydroxide (20%) and 10-parts hydrogen peroxide (3%) for 15 minutes. The cleared roots were then acidified using 5% hydrochloric acid to prepare them for staining, and then incubated in 0.05% trypan blue for 10–20 minutes depending on root thickness (Carrara et al., 2023; Comas et al., 2014).
The grid-intersect method was used to quantify AM colonization rates of the stained roots (Carrara et al., 2023; Giovannetti et al., 1980; McGonigle et al., 1990). While quantifying colonization rates in both stained (AM) and unstained (ECM) roots, we suspended the roots in lactoglycerol solution for preservation and to minimize movement. AM roots were distributed randomly across a 1 × 1 cm gridded Petri dish and evaluated for the presence or absence of mycorrhizal structures at each root-gridline intersection using a dissecting microscope at ~40X. The mycorrhizal colonization level of unstained ECM roots was calculated based on the percentage of root tips that were colonized after a visual inspection for ECM structures under a dissecting microscope (Bzdyk et al., 2019; Carrara et al., 2023).

Extracellular Enzyme Activity
We assayed the potential hydrolytic enzyme activities of nitrogen-releasing N-acetyl-glucosaminidase (NAG), phosphorus-releasing acid phosphatase (AP), and simple carbon-releasing β-glucosidase (BG) in the organic, rhizosphere and bulk soil fractions of our soil samples using a fluorometric method and 4-methylumbelliferyl-derived substrates (Carrara et al., 2023; Saiya-Cork et al., 2002). In addition we assayed the ligninolytic oxidative enzyme activities (phenol oxidase and peroxidase) in the organic, rhizosphere and bulk soil fractions of our soil samples using a colorimetric microplate method using 3,4-L-dihydroxyphenylalanine (Carrara et al., 2023; Saiya-Cork et al., 2002). Fluorescence was measured on a SpectraMax Gemini XPS microplate reader (Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA, USA) using SoftMax Pro Software (Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA, USA) at 365 nm excitation and 450 nm emission, and color change was quantified on an Infinite 200 PRO microplate reader (TECAN, Männedorf, Switzerland) at 460 nm.

Net Mineralization and Nitrification
For the July sampling date in both years, we quantified the net rates of N mineralization and nitrification in our soil samples by measuring changes in the concentrations of nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+) over 14 days. Inorganic N was extracted from either 1 g (organic horizon) or 2.5 g (mineral horizon) of soil in 10 mL of 2 M potassium chloride (KCl) solution. The extractions were performed before and after a 14–day incubation at room temperature to calculate the net N mineralization and nitrification rates based on initial and final concentrations of extractable NO3- and NH4+ pools in the soil (Finzi et al., 1998). The NO3− concentration in our samples was determined using a colorimetric microplate assay with a reagent containing a saturated solution of vanadium chloride (VCl3) and the Griess reagent (Hood-Nowotny et al., 2010; Miranda et al., 2001). Briefly, we dissolved 350 mg of VCl3 in 50 mL 1M HCl and combined this solution with 400 mL of nanopure water, 3.3 mL of 2% sulfanilamide in 1M HCl, and 3.3 mL of 0.2% N-(1-naphthyl)-ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (NED) in nanopure water. The NO3− samples were incubated for 5 hours at room temperature. The NH4+ concentration in our samples was determined using a colorimetric microplate assay method modified from Weatherburn (1967). Briefly, we combined a solution containing 6.8% sodium salicylate, 5% sodium citrate, 5% sodium tartrate, and 0.025% sodium nitroprusside with a bleach solution diluted 1:50 with 1.5 M sodium hydroxide. The NH4+ samples were incubated for 1 hour at room temperature. Color reaction was quantified on an Infinite 200 PRO microplate reader (TECAN, Männedorf, Switzerland) reader at 540 nm for NO3− and 650 nm for NH4+.
